newsitem.title: UK: UK-Asia cargo rates rise as summer schedules start.
newsitem.headline: UK-Asia cargo rates rise as summer schedules start.

text.p: Average air cargo rates ex-UK to the Middle East, Asia and Australasia have in most cases either risen or held firm over the past two weeks, a Reuters survey shows.

This is due to price increases traditionally introduced at the start of their summer schedules by carriers, the majority of which are retaining -- at least for the time being -- cargo fuel surcharges they imposed last October/November.
Another factor that has helped improve yields of late has been a softening of sterling against some currencies, boosting demand for UK exports by air, observers note.

The two ex-UK markets which have balked the trend are Korea, from where demand has fallen, and Australia, plagued by over-capacity fighting for a finite amount of available cargo that has kept downward pressure on rates.

"Perhaps the industrial troubles recently experienced in Korea have affected confidence there, but whatever the reasons, the Korean market has fallen back during the first three months of this year," said Frank Smith, UK cargo sales manager of Korean Air Lines.
"During the first quarter of 1996 we were turning business away because we couldn't accommodate it all. That's definitely not the case at present," he said.

This is not deterring privately-owned U.S. carrier Polar Air Cargo, which says it will start operating twice-weekly Boeing 747-200 freighter flights linking Manchester and Amsterdam with Korea and Japan from May 17.
"The UK-Korea airfreight market has always been strong in both directions and I see no problem in filling the capacity," said Polar's UK sales director Steve Lewis.

"There are now several major Korean companies either established or opening up plants in the north-east and north-west of England and in Wales," he added, explaining that Manchester's central location was one of the main reasons for its selection by the airline as the UK operating airport.

Cathay Pacific is another carrier looking at adding more capacity to Seoul, according to its northern UK cargo manager Ivor Llewellyn, who in the meantime is concentrating on what he described as the "booming" UK-Hong Kong market.
"It is exceptionally strong at the moment and there are no signs of demand easing," he said.

"This trend is unusual for this time of the year. The usual pre-Christmas business rush was followed by a good January and February for us and there was hardly any dip during Chinese New Year. The weakening of the pound is creating greater (ex-UK) export demand," Llewellyn noted.

All-cargo Air Hong Kong's UK country manager Bob Wetherill said that his carrier, 75 percent owned by Cathay, had experienced slow trading on its Manchester-HK 747F route in January/February but business had picked up in March "and is looking good for April".
The present four-times-weekly frequency will be increased to five from April 13 and Wetherill is looking forward to having the additional capacity available.
Britain-HK is supposedly a cabotage route restricted to each other's airlines, but it is well known that several other carriers also carry cargo between the two markets, analysts point out.
The cabotage status will end when Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight on June 30 and Dubai government-owned Emirates is one airline that eagerly awaits the chance to sell UK-HK cargo space openly.
"I expect to get good business on the route," said its UK cargo manager Ray Dissan.
All Nippon Airways' assistant UK cargo manager John O'Shea described the present state of the London-Tokyo market as "just steady", a sentiment echoed by Dave Church, his counterpart at Finnair.

"Japan is a very strong cargo destination for Scandinavia and so in the UK we are only allocated a limited amount of capacity on our twice-weekly MD-11 flights from Helsinki to Tokyo and Osaka," he said.
"If we get more space -- and the Osaka frequency will go up to three a week from May 18 -- then I am sure we could sell it," he added.
AHK's Wetherill is also welcoming the arrival of more ex-UK capacity Japan from today (Friday), when his carrier adds a third weekly 747-200 freighter flight between Hong Kong and Kansai, off Osaka.
"In the past, about six percent of our UK-originating cargo has been destined for Japan but, with the new Osaka frequency, we are optimistic this will grow significantly," he said.
Cathay's Llewellyn said that his business to Japan was "very strong", though restricted due to only limited capacity available.
Cargolux's UK manager Mark Boffee said Japan was his carrier's third biggest ex-UK cargo market after Singapore and Kuala Lumpur.
"There is a lot of competition but the market is expanding and we hope to keep our share," he said.
KAL's Frank Smith said he feeds some 50 to 60 tonnes of ex-UK cargo to Japan via Seoul.
"From Britain, we mainly move outsourced car industry materials to Japan. Last month, for example, we flew two 19-tonne loads of windscreens made here," he stated.

Local holidays currently underway in Taiwan have temporarily hit airfreight traffic from the UK, said Kimber Lee, deputy UK cargo manager of EVA Air, which operates three weekly London Heathrow-Bangkok-Taipei 747 Combi services.
"Shippers don't want to send their cargo to Taipei at this time only to have it wait around in warehouses on arrival. I expect the market to pick up from next week," he added.
Cathay's Llewellyn was pleased with his carrier's UK-Taiwan cargo performance. "We're doing very well and achieving rates slightly above the market average," he said.
From London to Manila, the average per kg/100 kg rate has risen two pence to 1.42 stg over the past fortnight.
Philippine Airlines' UK cargo spokesman Ian Workman says his carrier is "attracting some fair weights and getting good yields" for the route.
The UK-Bangkok market is described by EVA's Lee as "quite strong" at the present time and Tony Hardy, managing director of Lauda Air's UK cargo general sales agent Aviacargo, agreed.

"Lauda only operates two weekly Vienna-Bangkok-Hong Kong flights with 767-300s, which we feed with cargo on its Boeing 737 services from London Gatwick. We could fly more cargo to Bangkok if we had the space," he said.
Cargolux's Boffee said that for his UK operation, both Kuala Lumpur and, in particular Singapore were "very buoyant" markets at the moment.

Ray Dissan, of Emirates, noted that Singapore was one of the carrier's biggest ex-UK airfreight markets and he looked forward to bigger Boeing 777s taking over from Airbuses on its Dubai-Singapore route from May.
"Singapore is a very good market for us...business is very steady," he said.

For the first time, London-Beijing is included in Reuters' regular UK-Asia market report and average per kg/100 kg rate for the route this week stands at 1.45 stg. Less than 1.20 stg can be obtained per kg for 1,000 kg plus.
"While not as strong as Japan, Beijing is nevertheless a good steady market for us," said Finnair Cargo Dave Church.
"From Britain, we are sending a regular three to four tonnes a week on our twice-weekly, nonstop Helsinki-Beijing MD-11 services," he added.
China is a small market for Air Hong Kong in Britain, said Bob Wetherill, mainly because he finds it difficult to obtain sufficient capacity.
"At Hong Kong, we switch our China-bound freight to Dragonair flights on which we can only move 70kg pieces on lower-deck pallets," he stated.
Korean Air sends "a steady amount" of UK-originating cargo to China via Seoul, to several destinations including Shenzhen, Qingdao, Beijing and newly-opened Sanya, said Frank Smith in London.
With direct business to Korea declining slightly, he said he will in future have more space to sell onward to China, and even more specifically to Australia and New Zealand.

"Until recently, I haven't needed to cultivate new markets. But now, with the additional ex-UK space I have available and the start of a weekly KAL Seoul-Sydney MD-11 freighter service on April 2, that situation has changed," he said.

"I have an allocation of five tonnes on each of the new flights and on the first we received a block booking in the UK for a machinery consignment. The Australian market looks pretty buoyant for us here," he added.
This optimism is not reflected in the general sate of the marketplace, which has seen the average per kg/100 kg London-Sydney rate fall eight pence to 2.00 stg over recent weeks.
PAL's Workman blames, amongst others, British Airways for the downward spiral in rates to Australia. "They (BA) are currently charging stupid rates on the route," he said.
Added KAL's Smith: "BA is certainly involved in a big cargo rate sale at the moment."
In Britain, Cathay Pacific's only complaint about the Australian market is that its sales team cannot obtain enough capacity.
"We could fill what we are presently given five times over," said Ivor Llewellyn.

Emirates' Dissan said he is "desperate for extra capacity on all routes" and said he keenly awaits an increase in Manchester-Dubai frequencies to daily from the present five A310/A300 flights a week now in June.
In addition, the carrier is operating twice-daily Heathrow-Dubai 777 flights and a daily Airbus service from London Gatwick.
Air India's UK cargo manager Madhav Lokur continues to lament his lack of freight capacity from London to India.

"This market is booming but, with only 20 tonnes' capacity to sell each week, we are not able to take advantage of that," he said. --Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel +44 171 542 7706 Fax +5017 (c) Reuters Limited 1997
